_meta.model: claude-sonnet-4-6 (MODELS.SMART), 1 endpoint (/signal-vs-noise, fans out to 2 parallel calls merged server-side)
_meta.baseline_commit: signalvsnoise-v6 (WHAT AUTHORIZES THIS SENTENCE test + metaphor-reasoning guard + bottom-line lock, on top of v5/v4/v3/v2)
_meta.v5_note: v4's regex (CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE) was verb-conjugation-specific ('evidence shows/suggests/supports') and missed 12 of 13 real violations in the very next live test, a parenting/screen-time topic: 'the evidence tends to show,' 'observational research,' 'reviews of homework research... broadly recognized in ... literature,' 'researchers argue,' 'is associated with,' 'historically,' 'documented,' 'the evidence on X is Y.' Narrow verb-matching does not generalize across the many ways a model phrases 'I reviewed a body of evidence' — v5's list is now broad WORD/PHRASE matching (evidence/research + up to 3 words + a wide verb set, bare 'literature'/'historically'/'documented'/'associated with', etc.), verified against all 13 new violations plus 7 legitimate ALLOWED sentences (0 false positives, 0 false negatives) before shipping. ARCHITECTURE CHANGE: enforcement moved from a whole-CALL regenerate (v4) to PER-FIELD regenerate (v5) — enforceClaimModeFields()/regenerateField()/setAtPath() rewrite only the flagged sentence (cheap, MODELS.FAST, no JSON schema to fill), preserving everything the model got right instead of risking a whole-half regenerate trading one violation for a different one elsewhere. A field that still fails after its one regeneration attempt is left as-is and the EXISTING structural clean()-filter (unchanged) drops the enclosing item, same fallback as before. NEW: a traceability/scope-creep guard (rule 21 extended + 5 new outputGuard entries) — the same live test also introduced 'free-range parenting' and invented 'the core of free-range parenting' as a model-generated definition, neither of which the visitor raised (visitor supplied only screen time, tiger vs. free-range as a *label pair*, and homework — not a definition of any of them). Rule 21 now states an explicit traceability test (A: a supplied claim, B: a necessary distinction, C: an examined source — if none apply, don't write it). Also reinforced: rule 26 (new) — the_signal doesn't need one item per noise item, don't insert an unprompted epistemic lesson (e.g. 'before-and-after comparisons') the visitor didn't raise, don't invent an individual child/person to apply a population claim to (that belongs in what_general_claims_cant_decide, not the general bottom line). UI: a 'CLAIM ANALYSIS' mode badge with a tooltip now renders under ANALYZING (source_analysis/verified_research labels are unreachable today — this tool performs no live retrieval — and are not yet built; add them only if that capability is ever added). Catalog copy (src/data/tools.js description/seoDescription/primer.get) and svn_tagline reworded away from 'stronger evidence'/'genuinely unsettled' framing that implied the tool always has access to an evidence base, per the same principle as SOURCE MODE. Live-tested against the exact parenting/screen-time/homework scenario (0 banned-phrase hits, 0 field-fix regenerations needed — the strengthened prompt got it right without needing the backstop this time; the backstop's correctness was verified separately via 20 unit test cases against the regex directly). DO NOT revert to whole-call regeneration or narrow the banned-phrase list back to verb-conjugation matching — both were the specific gaps this pass closed.
_meta.v4_note: A THIRD 'final corrections' pass, same day as v3, found the identical literature-review-voice failure in a domain not yet tested — finance ('persistent tracking of fund returns... across multiple markets and asset classes,' 'the evidence covers funds that survived long enough to be measured,' a fabricated survivorship-bias limitation for a dataset never examined). Three prompt-only passes had not fully suppressed this, so v4 adds what they didn't have: a deterministic, ENGLISH-ONLY code-level backstop (see signal-vs-noise.js's CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE / findBannedPhrase / callClaimModeChecked) — every prose field is scanned against a fixed phrase list, a violating half is regenerated once with the exact offending phrase quoted back at it, and any array item that still violates after that is silently dropped rather than shown. The prompt still tries hard to get it right the first time (extensive new PERSONALITY rules, worked BAD/GOOD examples for the fee/valuation/real-estate/survivorship/professional-referral/ranking-against-unnamed-alternatives failures) — the regex is the guarantee, not a replacement for it. SCHEMA CHANGE: genuinely_debated (with nullable what_supports_one_view/another_view, introduced in v3) is REMOVED entirely and replaced by two separate top-level arrays: still_worth_verifying[] ({question, why_it_matters, what_would_help} — a genuinely unresolved GENERAL empirical question, never a fabricated two-sided debate) and what_general_claims_cant_decide[] (plain strings — person-specific questions a general analysis can never resolve, e.g. 'whether direct real estate fits your actual situation'). v3's null-views mechanism for person-dependent questions is superseded by this split, not extended. Response also gains analysis_mode ('claim_analysis', hard-locked in code, not model-self-reported) and sources_examined (always [] today — no source-paste feature exists). Caps changed: the_signal 4->3, still_worth_verifying capped at 2 (was genuinely_debated at 3), what_general_claims_cant_decide capped at 3, the_bottom_line.what_would_change_the_answer 2->3. i18n: svn_nuance reworded 'Limits:' -> "What it doesn't establish:"; svn_debated_header reworded 'Still Unsettled' -> 'Still Worth Verifying'; new keys svn_verify_why/svn_verify_would_help/svn_cant_decide_header; svn_one_view/svn_another_view/svn_why_unsettled are now orphaned (left in the locale files, no longer referenced in JSX — the two-sided-debate UI was removed, not relabeled). outputGuard.prohibit grew from 28 to 37 entries. DO NOT reverse the schema split or the code-level regex backstop — three prompt-only passes already proved insufficient on their own.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden signal-vs-noise). v2 (2026-09-09) fixed the health-domain instances of the tool implying a literature review it never performed. v3 (2026-09-10) fixed the SAME failure mode recurring in a non-health (career/labor) domain — 'wage data shows,' an invented MBA-recruiting market map, an invented causal mechanism for job-switching pay, a strawmanned 'follow your passion' critique, an extra unrequested career-advice claim, two noise_type mislabels, an unsupported publicity/selection-bias claim used to rebut an overclaim with another overclaim, debate-club phrasing, and a STILL UNSETTLED section forced into a two-sided-evidence shape it didn't have for a person-dependent question. v4 (same day) is documented in v4_note above. v5 (2026-09-10) is documented in v5_note above. v6 (2026-09-10) is documented in v6_note above.
_meta.prior_notes: v2 (2026-09-09) was a full owner-supplied rewrite: the v1 tool asserted "real consensus," named specific actors as "generating noise," and invoked specific research designs, biomarkers, genetic variants, and validation findings from memory as though it had performed a sourced evidence review — exactly the authority the tool was never in a position to claim. Schema changed completely from v1 (why_this_field_is_noisy -> framing; the_signal.items[].why_we_know_this -> basis; .the_nuance -> limits; genuinely_debated[].side_a/side_b -> what_supports_one_view/what_supports_another_view (later removed entirely in v4); the_noise[] gained what_the_evidence_supports_instead alongside renamed what_went_wrong (was the_problem); the_bottom_line's three single-string fields became three arrays; sources_of_noise[].actor/incentive/how_to_spot_it -> source_type/how_it_distorts/how_to_recognize_it, no longer naming an accused actor). Guards added that pass: NO_QUOTE_RULE, router.outputStandard='v2' + outputGuard, and a post-guard structural validation pass (see code comment: the guard mutates its argument in place and its repair pass can leave a field incomplete despite instructions not to).
_meta.v6_note: A FOURTH 'final corrections' pass, sleep domain, confirmed the deterministic claim_analysis mode switch (v4) had finally killed the fake-literature-review voice, but found a narrower, different failure: unlabeled empirical premises imported from memory that never use evidence-provenance wording at all, so CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE cannot catch them ('most adults need roughly 7-9 hours', 'light exposure is one input to the body's circadian timing system', 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness'), plus a logical non-sequitur reasoning backward from a metaphor's usefulness to a fact about the thing it describes ('if a single recovery night fully erased all sleep debt, the metaphor wouldn't be useful'), plus a bottom line that broke back into sleep/parenting/finance guidance and invented personal context nobody supplied in what_would_change_the_answer. FIX (prompt-level, not regex — this class of error has no stable lexical marker a regex can key on): new rule 27 ('WHAT AUTHORIZES THIS SENTENCE?') gives the model an explicit 3-way test before writing any factual sentence — A. USER_CLAIM (the visitor supplied it), B. LOGIC (follows from the claim's own structure, no empirical finding needed), C. LABELED_BACKGROUND (genuinely ordinary vocabulary-only background, used sparingly, never the central empirical answer) — rewrite or remove if none apply. New rule 28 fixes the metaphor non-sequitur (critique what a metaphor fails to establish, never reason backward from 'what would make it useful'). New rule 29 locks the bottom line to summarizing the claim analysis only, and reserves personal-situation language in what_would_change_the_answer for when the visitor actually supplied enough personal context to identify a real gap. NORTH STAR gained a prepended 3-line frame: use knowledge to understand the claim, logic to test it, evidence to settle it. TRAP HIT AND FIXED DURING THIS PASS: the rule 27/29 illustrative BAD examples quoted the exact attractor phrase 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness' TWICE, verbatim — live testing showed the model echoing that near-verbatim phrase straight into output (a known trap: worked BAD-example text gets copied rather than avoided, see deftbrain-voice-prompt-traps memory). Fixed by rewriting both examples to describe the ERROR PATTERN in the abstract (no specific number, no specific mechanism, no specific magnitude-of-benefit claim to copy) plus an explicit 'this is illustrating a pattern, not a script — a close paraphrase is the same violation' instruction. Verified 0 banned-phrase / 0 attractor-phrase hits across 3 consecutive live regenerations of the exact sleep scenario after the reword (the run before the reword produced the attractor phrase; the runs after did not). UI: added a visible 'No outside sources reviewed' sub-label beside the CLAIM ANALYSIS badge (the existing badge only had it in a hover tooltip, poor discoverability) and a 'Research These Claims' disclosure at the end of results, built from still_worth_verifying (falling back to what_would_change_the_answer) with one external search-engine link per open question — pure frontend, no new backend capability. This is deliberately NOT a live-retrieval / verified-research mode: the tool has no wired search or fetch capability, and building real retrieval is an infrastructure decision (external dependency, cost per request, latency, reliability) flagged to the owner rather than silently built or silently dropped, same position as the v5 note. i18n: svn_honest_uncertainty relabeled '? What Could Change the Answer' -> '? What Would Help' across all 13 languages (claim-analysis mode is never about the visitor's personal situation, so the more evidence-focused label is now the default; a personalized 'what could change the answer' framing would need a genuinely supplied personal-context case, which this tool does not yet branch on). New keys: svn_no_sources_reviewed, svn_research_these_claims, svn_research_intro, svn_search_this (13 languages each). DO NOT re-quote a specific number, mechanism, or magnitude figure in rule 27/28/29's illustrative examples — describe the pattern, never the sentence.

input.conflictingAdvice: Index funds always win vs. active management can beat the market, time in market beats timing the market vs. valuations matter, real estate vs. stocks

the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Low-cost index funds avoid the problem of picking the right manager and generally charge less than actively managed alternatives. Whether they outperform in any specific period, market, or asset class is a narrower question the slogan does not answer.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The word 'always' converts a structural argument about costs and manager selection into a universal guarantee across all time periods, markets, and investor situations. The logic of the cost argument holds without needing 'always.'
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: A fee deducted from a return reduces that return relative to the same investment without the fee. Over time, that difference can compound. That arithmetic is straightforward and does not require the 'always' claim.

the_noise.claim: Time in the market beats timing the market
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Successfully moving out of the market before declines and back in before recoveries requires getting multiple decisions right in sequence. That makes 'time the market' a much stronger prescription than simply recognizing that staying invested avoids certain compounding mistakes. Staying invested is easier to execute reliably than a correct sequence of in-and-out calls.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The slogan treats 'timing the market' as a single decision, when it is at minimum two decisions (when to exit, when to re-enter) that must both be correct. It also does not address situations where an investor's actual time horizon, liquidity need, or risk exposure makes some adjustment genuinely appropriate — not as market prediction, but as personal circumstance.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: The core point — that repeated attempts to predict short-term market movements introduce additional decision points where things can go wrong — is structurally sound without needing to be stated as an absolute rule.

the_noise.noise_label: True in one sense, misused in another
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: The price paid for an investment is relevant to its potential return — that much follows from basic arithmetic. But 'valuations matter' becomes a stronger claim when it is used to imply that a current valuation reading tells you when to enter or exit the market. Those are different propositions.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Recognizing that price affects expected return does not supply a reliable buy or sell rule. The slogan is accurate as a statement about price and value, but gets extended into a timing instruction it cannot support on its own.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Price is not irrelevant to an investment's future return. That part of the claim stands without requiring it to serve as a market-timing signal.

the_noise.claim: Real estate vs. stocks — one clearly beats the other
the_noise.noise_label: The comparison hides what actually differs
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Stocks and direct real estate expose an investor to different combinations of liquidity, concentration, leverage, costs, management demands, and cash flows. A 'which asset class wins?' framing can obscure those structural differences, which are often more decision-relevant than a return comparison.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Changing which costs are included (leverage, transaction costs, maintenance, vacancy, taxes), which time period is selected, and whether leverage effects are accounted for can materially change any comparison. A simple head-to-head return claim is sensitive to each of those choices.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Both asset classes can be legitimate ways to build wealth. The useful question is how their structural differences fit a particular investor's situation — not which one won over some past window.

supported_takeaways: The cost argument for index funds is structurally sound: a lower fee means more of the return stays with the investor, and that difference can compound. That conclusion does not require 'always win.'

Staying invested avoids a specific compounding risk — making multiple sequential timing decisions that must each go right. That is a meaningful practical point, even without claiming that valuations are irrelevant.

The real estate vs. stocks question turns substantially on structural factors — leverage, liquidity, concentration, costs, management demands — that a simple return comparison can hide. Identifying those factors is more useful than declaring a winner.
treat_skeptically: Any investing claim that uses 'always,' 'never,' or 'beats' without specifying the time period, costs included, and investor situation — the strength of those words is rarely earned.
Valuation arguments that slide from 'price affects expected return' into 'therefore exit now' — the first is a matter of arithmetic, the second is a timing claim that requires much more to support.

Return comparisons between real estate and stocks that do not spell out their assumptions about leverage, transaction costs, and management input — changing those assumptions can reverse the comparison.
what_would_change_the_answer: Your actual time horizon, liquidity needs, and how concentrated your exposure already is matter more to these questions than the general claims do — the claims analyzed here do not resolve what makes sense for a specific situation.

If any of these claims were encountered in a specific article, fund pitch, or comparison tool, examining what costs and assumptions were included or excluded would clarify how much to rely on its conclusion.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A principle that holds under specific conditions gets compressed into a universal rule. The conditions that limited the original claim disappear, and the slogan travels further than its reasoning supports.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim uses 'always,' 'beats,' or 'wins' without specifying time period, asset type, cost structure, or investor situation. Ask: under what conditions would this not hold?

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A comparison between two asset classes or strategies is presented as a straightforward factual result, but the conclusion depends heavily on which costs, leverage assumptions, time windows, and return components were included. Different choices produce different outcomes.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A comparison that presents a single winner without disclosing its assumptions about leverage, fees, time period, and what counts as a return. Ask: what would change if those inputs were different?

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A sound general principle (price affects return; staying invested avoids certain errors) gets extended into a specific action instruction (exit now; never adjust). The instruction requires more support than the principle provides.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim moves from a general observation to a specific buy, sell, or hold recommendation without explaining what additional evidence or reasoning bridges the gap.

output.topic_as_understood: Three recurring investing debates: whether index funds reliably outperform active management, whether staying invested beats trying to time the market, and whether real estate or stocks is the better investment
output.framing: Each of these debates packages a genuine insight inside a claim that is broader than the insight warrants. The useful work is separating the part that holds up from the part that was added through certainty or generalization.

items.claim: A fee deducted from an investment reduces its net return relative to the same investment without that fee, and that difference compounds over time.
items.basis: This follows from arithmetic. If two investments produce the same gross return and one charges a higher ongoing fee, the net return of the higher-fee investment will be lower by at least that amount each period, and the gap widens as compounding proceeds. Low-cost index funds avoid the manager-selection problem and generally charge less than actively managed alternatives. The stronger claim — that index funds always win — does not follow from this, because it converts a structural cost observation into a universal performance guarantee.
items.limits: This establishes that costs matter to net returns. It does not establish that any specific active fund will underperform, that manager skill cannot offset costs in a given case, or that low cost is the only factor relevant to choosing between funds.

items.claim: Successfully moving out of the market before declines and back in before recoveries requires getting multiple decisions right under uncertainty, which makes 'time the market' a substantially stronger prescription than simply recognizing that price paid is relevant to expected return.
items.basis: This follows from what the strategy requires. A market-timing approach demands at least two correct calls per cycle — when to exit and when to re-enter — and errors in either direction reduce the benefit. Recognizing that valuations are not irrelevant is a much weaker claim than asserting a reliable timing rule can be derived from them. Both can be true simultaneously: price paid can matter to long-run expected return without that mattering translating into an actionable signal.
items.limits: This does not establish that valuations have no predictive relevance to long-run returns, nor that staying invested is always correct regardless of an investor's time horizon, liquidity needs, or specific circumstances.

items.claim: Stocks and direct real estate expose an investor to meaningfully different combinations of liquidity, concentration, leverage, management demands, and cash flow structure — a simple 'which asset class wins?' comparison tends to obscure those differences.
items.basis: This follows from what the assets are. A stock in a diversified fund can typically be sold in seconds; a property cannot. Direct real estate is often purchased with leverage, which amplifies both gains and losses in a way a comparison to unleveraged stock returns would not capture. Direct real estate also requires ongoing management time and carries transaction costs that are substantially higher than those of most stock transactions. A return comparison that does not account for these structural differences is comparing different things.
items.limits: This does not establish which asset class produces better returns for any given investor or period. It establishes that fair comparison requires accounting for the structural differences, not that either asset class is superior.

still_worth_verifying.question: Over what range of time horizons and market conditions does the cost advantage of passive indexing translate into a net performance advantage, and how consistent is that relationship across different fund categories and geographies?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The 'index funds always win' claim depends on this being stable and broad — if the cost-to-performance relationship varies substantially by category, period, or market structure, the universal version of the claim weakens further.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Long-horizon, category-level comparisons of net returns between passive and active funds across multiple market environments, broken down by asset class and geography, would help assess how stable and broad the relationship actually is.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether the cost advantage of index funds outweighs other considerations for any specific fund, account type, or investment goal you are evaluating.
Whether your time horizon, liquidity needs, and circumstances make staying fully invested the right posture, or whether some allocation to cash or other assets is appropriate for your situation.
Whether direct real estate, REITs, stocks, or some combination makes sense given your actual capital, tolerance for illiquidity, appetite for active management, and existing holdings.

input.conflictingAdvice: Indexfonds gewinnen immer vs. aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen, Zeit im Markt schlaegt Markt-Timing vs. Bewertungen sind wichtig

the_noise.noise_label: Aus einem strukturellen Vorteil wird eine Garantie
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Kostengünstige Indexfonds vermeiden das Problem der Managerauswahl und belasten die Rendite mit geringeren laufenden Kosten als aktiv verwaltete Fonds. Daraus folgt kein Versprechen, dass sie in jedem Zeitraum, in jeder Anlageklasse oder unter jeder Marktbedingung besser abschneiden.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Der Anspruch verwandelt einen strukturellen Kostenvorteil in eine zeitlose Garantie. Ein niedrigerer Kostenblock verbessert die Nettorendite gegenüber dem identischen Investment mit höherem Kostenblock – das ist Arithmetik, kein empirisch bewiesenes 'Immer-Gewinnen'. Das Wort 'immer' trägt eine Beweislast, die kein strukturelles Argument erfüllen kann.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Eine Gebühr, die vom investierten Kapital abgezogen wird, schmälert die Nettorendite gegenüber demselben Investment ohne diese Gebühr. Dieser Unterschied kann sich über Zeit verstärken. Das ist der legitime Kern des Arguments.

the_noise.claim: Aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Dass aktives Management den Markt schlagen kann, ist logisch möglich – Märkte sind nicht perfekt, und einzelne Entscheidungen können sich als richtig erweisen. Ob ein bestimmter Fonds oder Manager es tut, hängt von Kosten, Zeitraum, Anlageklasse und Glück versus Können ab. Die allgemeine Aussage 'kann schlagen' rechtfertigt weder die Wahl eines bestimmten aktiven Produkts noch den Verzicht auf kostengünstigere Alternativen.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Die Aussage ist technisch wahr, aber als Handlungsanleitung zu schwach, um nützlich zu sein. Sie sagt nichts darüber, wie wahrscheinlich es ist, im Voraus den richtigen Manager zu identifizieren, welche Kosten dabei entstehen, oder ob der Vorteil nach Gebühren bestehen bleibt. Eine Möglichkeit zu benennen ist keine Empfehlung, auf sie zu setzen.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Aktives Management ist nicht per Definition unmöglich. Es gibt Marktsegmente, in denen Informationsvorsprünge oder Spezialisierung theoretisch einen Mehrwert erzeugen könnten. Ob und wo das zuverlässig gilt, ist eine offene Frage, keine gesicherte Grundlage für eine Kaufentscheidung.

the_noise.noise_label: Preis ist relevant wird zu: Timing-Regel
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Der Preis, den man für ein Investment zahlt, ist für die mögliche zukünftige Rendite relevant – das folgt aus der Logik des Kaufens. Daraus folgt aber nicht, dass gängige Bewertungsmaßstäbe verlässlich anzeigen, wann man ein- oder aussteigen sollte.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: 'Bewertungen sind wichtig' ist, für sich genommen, kaum bestreitbar. Das Problem entsteht, wenn daraus eine Timing-Anweisung abgeleitet wird: 'Bewertungen sind hoch, also nicht kaufen' oder 'Bewertungen sind niedrig, also kaufen'. Das sind zwei unterschiedliche Aussagen. Letztere setzt voraus, dass Bewertungsmaßstäbe kurzfristige oder mittelfristige Marktbewegungen zuverlässig vorhersagen – eine deutlich stärkere Behauptung als die erste.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Preis ist nicht irrelevant. Der Preis, zu dem man kauft, beeinflusst die Rendite – das ist keine Kontroverse. Die Kontroverse betrifft die Frage, ob verfügbare Bewertungskennzahlen als praktisches Timing-Instrument taugen.

supported_takeaways: Kostengünstige Indexfonds haben einen strukturellen Vorteil gegenüber teureren Alternativen: Niedrigere Kosten bedeuten höhere Nettorendite bei sonst gleichen Bedingungen. Das folgt aus Arithmetik, nicht aus einer Renditegarantie.

Aktives Management ist nicht grundsätzlich ausgeschlossen, aber 'es ist möglich' reicht nicht als Begründung für ein konkretes Produkt. Die relevante Frage ist, ob der erwartete Mehrwert die höheren Kosten nach Gebühren übertrifft – und das lässt sich im Voraus kaum zuverlässig beurteilen.

Bewertungen und Markt-Timing sind unterschiedliche Konzepte. Dass der Kaufpreis die potenzielle Rendite beeinflusst, ist unbestritten. Ob Bewertungskennzahlen als Timing-Signal funktionieren, ist eine eigenständige, offenere Frage.
treat_skeptically: Jede Formulierung, die einen strukturellen oder statistischen Vorteil in eine Garantie verwandelt – 'gewinnt immer', 'schlägt immer' oder 'funktioniert immer'.
Timing-Empfehlungen, die aus Bewertungsbeobachtungen abgeleitet werden, ohne zu erklären, auf welchem Zeithorizont und mit welcher Treffsicherheit diese Verbindung gilt.
Das Argument 'aktives Management kann schlagen' als Begründung für ein konkretes Produkt – die logische Möglichkeit ist kein Kaufargument.
what_would_change_the_answer: Wenn ein konkreter Fonds, Zeitraum oder Bewertungsmaßstab genannt wird, lässt sich die jeweilige Aussage gezielter prüfen – allgemeine Analyseprinzipien ersetzen diese produktspezifische Prüfung nicht.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Komplexe, bedingungsabhängige Zusammenhänge werden in einprägsame Sätze komprimiert. Dabei fallen die Bedingungen weg, unter denen die Aussage gilt – und der Satz wird breiter weitergegeben, als er gemeint war.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Absolute Formulierungen ohne Angabe von Bedingungen, Zeiträumen oder Ausnahmen: 'gewinnt immer', 'schlägt immer', 'funktioniert immer'.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Dass etwas möglich ist, wird als hinreichende Begründung behandelt, darauf zu setzen. Der Schritt von 'kann passieren' zu 'wird wahrscheinlich passieren' oder 'ist für mich wahrscheinlich erreichbar' wird übersprungen.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Aussagen, die 'kann' oder 'ist möglich' als Kaufargument präsentieren, ohne Wahrscheinlichkeit, Kosten oder Bedingungen zu nennen.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Eine berechtigte Beobachtung (z. B. dass Bewertungen die Rendite beeinflussen) wird direkt in eine Handlungsanleitung umgewandelt, ohne zu prüfen, ob die Beobachtung als zuverlässiges Signal für konkrete Kauf- oder Verkaufszeitpunkte taugt.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Wenn auf eine allgemeine Aussage über Preise oder Bewertungen unmittelbar folgt, wann man kaufen oder verkaufen sollte – ohne dass der Zwischenschritt begründet wird.

output.topic_as_understood: Drei verbreitete Investitionsthesen im Vergleich: Indexfonds gegen aktives Management, Zeit im Markt gegen Markt-Timing, und die Frage, ob Bewertungen eine Rolle spielen.
output.framing: Alle drei Thesen bewegen sich auf unterschiedlichen Ebenen: Die erste betrifft Produktwahl, die zweite Verhalten über die Zeit, die dritte die Frage, ob der Einstiegszeitpunkt überhaupt messbar relevant ist. Eine Behauptung kann auf einer Ebene zutreffen und auf einer anderen trotzdem zu weit gehen.

items.claim: Indexfonds vermeiden das Problem der Managerwahl und erheben in der Regel geringere Gebühren als aktiv verwaltete Fonds. Eine Gebühr, die vom investierten Kapital abgezogen wird, reduziert die Nettorendite gegenüber derselben Anlage ohne diese Gebühr — und dieser Unterschied kann sich über Zeit durch Zinseszinseffekte vergrößern.
items.basis: Dies folgt aus der Arithmetik des Zinseszinses: Eine dauerhaft geringere Kostenbasis erhöht den Anteil der Rendite, der im Portfolio verbleibt. Das Managerproblem — ob ein bestimmter aktiver Manager den Markt zuverlässig übertrifft — entfällt bei einem Indexfonds per Konstruktion, weil er den Markt abbildet statt ihn zu schlagen.
items.limits: Daraus folgt nicht, dass Indexfonds 'immer gewinnen'. Es folgt nicht, dass kein aktiver Manager den Markt schlagen kann. Es folgt nicht, dass Indexfonds für jede Anlagestrategie, jeden Zeithorizont oder jede steuerliche Situation die überlegene Wahl sind.

items.claim: Markt-Timing als zuverlässige Strategie setzt voraus, dass mehrere Entscheidungen hintereinander richtig getroffen werden: wann man aussteigt, wann man wieder einsteigt, und dies konsistent über viele Marktzyklen. Je mehr solche Entscheidungen richtig sein müssen, desto anspruchsvoller wird die Bedingung.
items.basis: Dies folgt aus der Struktur des Timings selbst: Wer den Markt verlässt, muss mindestens zwei Zeitpunkte richtig bestimmen — den Ausstieg und den Wiedereinstieg. Jede zusätzliche Timing-Entscheidung multipliziert die Anforderung an die Treffsicherheit. Das ist keine Aussage darüber, was Anleger im Durchschnitt tun, sondern über das, was die Strategie strukturell verlangt.
items.limits: Daraus folgt nicht, dass Markt-Timing niemals funktioniert oder dass Bewertungen für Anlageentscheidungen irrelevant sind. Es folgt nicht, dass 'einfach investiert bleiben' unter allen Umständen die bessere Entscheidung ist — das hängt vom tatsächlichen Zeithorizont, der Liquiditätssituation und den konkreten Kosten ab.

items.claim: Der Preis, den man für eine Anlage zahlt, ist rechnerisch relevant für die potenzielle Rendite: Bei gleichen künftigen Erträgen führt ein höherer Einstiegspreis zu einer niedrigeren prozentualen Rendite. 'Bewertungen spielen eine Rolle' ist in diesem rechnerischen Sinne zutreffend.
items.basis: Dies folgt aus der Definition von Rendite: Rendite ergibt sich aus dem Verhältnis von Ertrag zu eingesetztem Kapital. Steigt der Einstiegspreis bei gleichem künftigem Ertrag, sinkt die Rendite. Das ist keine empirische Behauptung über Märkte, sondern eine arithmetische Beziehung.
items.limits: Daraus folgt nicht, dass gängige Bewertungsmaßstäbe zuverlässig anzeigen, wann der richtige Zeitpunkt zum Kauf oder Verkauf ist. 'Bewertungen spielen eine Rolle' und 'Bewertungsmaßstäbe liefern ein verlässliches Timing-Signal' sind zwei verschiedene Behauptungen. Die zweite ist aus dem arithmetischen Argument allein nicht ableitbar.

still_worth_verifying.question: Liefern verfügbare Bewertungsmaßstäbe — wie Kurs-Gewinn-Verhältnisse oder ähnliche Kennzahlen — über unterschiedliche Marktphasen und Zeithorizonte hinweg ein zuverlässiges Timing-Signal, das nach Transaktionskosten und Steuern einen Vorteil gegenüber dem Investiertbleiben ergibt?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Wenn ja, wäre 'Zeit im Markt schlägt Timing' als allgemeine Regel zu schwach; wenn nein, bleibt die Timing-Kritik strukturell begründet.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Langfristige, vergleichende Daten zu Anlagestrategien, die auf Bewertungssignalen basieren, unter Einbezug aller relevanten Kosten und verschiedener Marktregimes — nicht nur günstiger Zeitfenster.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Ob Indexfonds oder aktiv verwaltete Fonds für deine konkrete Situation sinnvoller sind — das hängt von deinem Zeithorizont, der steuerlichen Behandlung in deinem Fall, verfügbaren Produkten und deinen tatsächlichen Kosten ab.

Ob du in einer bestimmten Marktphase investiert bleiben, einsteigen oder abwarten solltest — das erfordert Informationen über deine Liquiditätssituation, deinen Anlagezeitraum und was du tatsächlich mit dem Kapital vorhast.

Ob ein bestimmter aktiv verwalteter Fonds seine Mehrkosten durch Mehrrendite rechtfertigen kann — das lässt sich aus allgemeinen Thesen nicht ableiten und erfordert die Prüfung des konkreten Produkts.

input.conflictingAdvice: Screen time is destroying kids vs. it depends on content, tiger parenting vs. free-range, homework helps vs. homework is harmful

the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Screen time is not a single thing. Watching a video call with a grandparent, playing an open-ended puzzle game, and passively scrolling algorithmically curated short clips are different activities with different demands on attention, social engagement, and sleep. A claim about 'screen time' that does not specify the activity, the amount, the child's age, or the outcome being measured cannot be evaluated as written.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim collapses a broad category of activities into one variable and assigns it a single causal verdict. That framing makes the claim look more settled than it is, because it bundles together cases that may differ substantially in what they do and do not affect.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Some uses of screens — particularly those that displace sleep, physical activity, or face-to-face interaction, or expose children to distressing or age-inappropriate content — plausibly carry real costs. That more specific concern is worth taking seriously.

the_noise.noise_label: Parenting style label applied as a universal prescription
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: High parental expectations and involvement can matter, but the outcomes of any parenting approach depend heavily on the specific practices involved, the child's temperament, the cultural and economic context, and what 'success' is being measured. A label like 'tiger parenting' bundles together high expectations, authoritarian control, emotional pressure, and intensive involvement — components that may not all work the same way or in the same direction, which means the label itself obscures which parts, if any, are actually driving the results someone observes.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim converts a cultural observation or a parenting label into a transferable prescription. Even if high-achievement outcomes appear together with certain practices in certain contexts, noticing that pattern does not establish that the practices caused the outcomes, rather than both reflecting shared advantages, parental selection, family resources, or other conditions that might produce success independently.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Expectations and engaged parenting can matter. The problem is asserting that a specific cluster of demanding practices reliably produces success across children and contexts.

the_noise.noise_label: Both sides of a debate stated as universals
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: 'Homework helps' and 'homework is harmful' are both incomplete as general claims. What homework does — if anything — depends on the age of the child, the subject, the amount assigned, whether the child has support to complete it, and what outcome is being measured (test scores, retention, stress, family conflict, or something else). A claim that does not specify these cannot be confirmed or refuted.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Each side of this debate treats one pattern — if it is even a consistent pattern — as a universal rule. The claim's scope (all homework, all children, all outcomes) exceeds what any aggregate finding could responsibly support.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Whether a particular homework practice is useful or counterproductive is a real question. That question just cannot be answered for 'homework' in the abstract.

supported_takeaways: For screen time, content and context do the work that total-hours measurements cannot. Asking what a child is doing on a screen, and what it is displacing, is more useful than a blanket time limit.

For parenting style debates, the label ('tiger,' 'free-range') is less informative than the specific practices it refers to — and what those practices produce likely varies with the child's temperament and circumstances.
For homework, the general debate ('helps or harms') is less useful than the specific question: for this child, at this age, in this subject, is this amount of homework serving its intended purpose?
treat_skeptically: Any claim that assigns a single outcome — positive or negative — to 'screen time,' 'tiger parenting,' or 'homework' without specifying age, amount, type, and what outcome is being measured.
Parenting prescriptions that present a cultural pattern as a universally transferable formula, especially when the proposed mechanism (why it works) is not spelled out.
what_would_change_the_answer: Knowing the specific studies or sources behind these claims would allow the claims they actually make — and the evidence they actually present — to be evaluated rather than the slogans alone.

sources_of_noise.source_type: Category labels applied to heterogeneous behaviors
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: When a single label ('screen time,' 'tiger parenting,' 'homework') covers a wide range of distinct activities or practices, findings about one subset can be stated as if they apply to the whole category. The label does the work of unifying things that may not belong together.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A claim uses a broad label but does not specify which version of the behavior, which age group, which outcomes, or which conditions the finding applies to.

sources_of_noise.source_type: Population averages presented as individual prescriptions
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Even a real pattern at the population level — if one exists — does not tell you what will happen with a specific child in a specific context. Parenting advice often moves from 'children in this group tended toward this outcome' to 'therefore you should do this,' skipping the step of establishing that the conditions generalize.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The advice drops all qualifications and addresses 'your child' or 'all children' without naming the specific conditions under which the finding held.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Parenting approaches get credit for salient outcomes — high test scores, elite college admissions, professional achievement — while costs to other outcomes (stress, family relationships, intrinsic motivation, wellbeing) may receive less attention in the same account. This is a possibility to watch for, not an established pattern.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A parenting claim is supported mainly by pointing to impressive outcomes in specific children, without addressing what was also present or absent in those cases, or what range of outcomes occurred across similar approaches.

output.topic_as_understood: Whether popular parenting prescriptions — limits on screen time, authoritarian vs. permissive styles, and homework — are supported strongly enough to treat as reliable general rules
output.framing: Each of these debates collapses a conditional question into a universal one. The useful work is identifying which conditions actually change the answer, rather than picking a side in the slogan version of each dispute.

items.claim: Screen time is not a single thing, and treating total hours as the only variable that matters omits conditions likely to change the outcome
items.basis: By definition, 'screen time' covers passive consumption, interactive communication, creative production, and educational engagement — activities with different cognitive and social demands. A blanket hour-count treats these as equivalent, which the categories themselves do not support. Content, context (solo vs. with others), and what the screen time displaces are all distinct variables that the simple claim ignores.
items.limits: This does not establish that unlimited or any particular kind of screen use is harmless. It only establishes that the claim 'screen time is destroying kids' is too coarse to be reliably actionable as stated.

items.claim: 'Homework helps' and 'homework is harmful' are both incomplete claims unless they specify age, amount, type of work, and the outcome being measured
items.basis: This follows from what the two claims are actually asserting. 'Helps' and 'harmful' both require specifying: helps or harms what outcome (test scores, interest in learning, family stress, sleep), for which age group, in what amount, and compared to what alternative use of that time. Without those conditions, the two slogans are not in disagreement about any specific proposition — they are just asserting opposite verdicts on an underspecified question.
items.limits: This does not settle what the right amount or type of homework is at any particular age — it only identifies why the debate as framed cannot produce a useful answer.

items.claim: Consistent warmth and clear expectations are not in tension with each other as parenting features, and the tiger-vs.-free-range framing treats them as opposites when they are not
items.basis: This follows from what each label is typically used to mean. 'Tiger parenting' emphasizes high demands; 'free-range' emphasizes autonomy and low control. Framing them as the two options implies that high expectations and high responsiveness are mutually exclusive, which the definitions do not require. A parent can hold high expectations while remaining responsive, or grant autonomy while remaining warm. The either/or presentation creates a false choice.
items.limits: This does not establish which combination of warmth and structure produces the best outcomes, or how to define 'best outcomes' — those remain genuinely contested. It only identifies that the binary framing misrepresents the actual dimensions.

still_worth_verifying.question: Whether specific categories of screen content or use — for example, fast-paced passive video vs. interactive communication vs. creative tools — produce meaningfully different developmental outcomes, and whether those differences vary by age
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: If content type and age interact, that would give parents a more actionable basis for decisions than total-hour limits alone — but it would also make simple rules harder to apply
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Long-term studies comparing children with similar total screen exposure but different content mixes and use contexts, with outcomes measured beyond test scores to include sleep, attention, and social development

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether the amount and type of homework your child currently has is appropriate depends on their age, what subjects are involved, how much time it actually takes them, and what it is displacing — general population-level claims cannot answer that
Whether your child's current screen use is a concern depends on what they are doing, how it affects sleep and other activities, and your child's individual response — not on hours alone

input.topic: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
input.conflictingAdvice: My coworker says blue light glasses fixed her insomnia. Another friend says sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends, but my doctor said catching up on weekends helps.

the_noise.claim: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Sleep need is a real phenomenon — most adults require a meaningful amount of nightly sleep, and consistently getting too little can impair functioning. But stating it as exactly 8 hours for every person converts a rough population-level figure into a precise individual prescription it was never designed to bear.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: A general average or guideline range becomes a universal, precise threshold applied to all individuals equally. People vary in their sleep requirements, and functioning well on somewhat more or less than 8 hours does not by itself indicate a problem. The word 'exactly' is what the claim cannot support.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Sleep duration matters. If someone sleeps chronically short, their functioning suffers—that is a straightforward cause-and-effect concern, not a finding from studies. A consistent nightly sleep target is a reasonable goal for that reason. The error is the precision and universality, not the underlying concern about sleep quantity.

the_noise.claim: Blue light glasses fixed my coworker's insomnia
the_noise.noise_label: Single anecdote presented as a general remedy
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Insomnia can have multiple contributing factors. Reducing exposure to bright light before sleep is a plausible behavioral change worth considering. Whether blue-light-filtering glasses specifically drive improvement — rather than other changes in routine, reduced screen engagement, placebo effect, or simple expectation — cannot be determined from one person's experience.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: One person's outcome is reported as a cause-and-effect conclusion. An individual case cannot isolate which element produced the change, how much it helped, or whether the same intervention would help anyone else. 'Fixed her insomnia' also implies a complete and durable resolution that a single anecdote cannot establish.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Light exposure before sleep is a real variable in sleep quality for some people. The reported experience may reflect a genuine improvement — the problem is attributing it with confidence to blue light glasses specifically, and treating it as a transferable remedy.

the_noise.claim: Sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends
the_noise.noise_label: Absolute rule from a conditional question
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Whether, and how fully, lost sleep can be recovered through later sleep is a genuinely open question. 'Sleep debt' is a metaphor; what the metaphor does not establish on its own is whether recovery is possible, how complete it is, or what timescale applies. Stating flatly that it 'cannot' be repaid presents one position on an unsettled question as a settled fact.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim converts an open, nuanced question into a categorical prohibition. Even if recovery sleep does not fully restore all effects of prior sleep loss, 'does not fully restore' and 'cannot be repaid at all' are different claims. The absolute framing outruns what the question itself supports.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: There are real reasons to be cautious about treating weekends as a reliable reset for chronic short sleep. The concern behind the claim is legitimate. The error is stating the stronger, absolute version as though it were established.

the_noise.claim: Catching up on sleep on weekends helps
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Additional sleep when you are sleep-deprived may improve how you feel and function in the short term. Whether it fully reverses accumulated sleep loss, and whether irregular sleep timing introduces its own costs, are separate questions the simple claim does not address.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim is framed as an unqualified endorsement. It omits the question of whether recovery is complete and whether shifting sleep timing on weekends relative to weekdays carries its own effects on circadian consistency. A partial or short-term benefit is not the same as a clean restoration of what was lost.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: More sleep when underslept plausibly helps in some respects. The claim is not simply wrong — it is incomplete in ways that matter when deciding how much to rely on weekend recovery as a strategy.

supported_takeaways: The '8 hours exactly' framing is too precise. Sleep need varies across people, and a rough general target is not the same as a universal exact requirement that applies identically to everyone.
Your coworker's experience with blue light glasses is real to her, but one person's outcome cannot tell you whether the glasses caused the improvement or whether the same change would help you.

Your friend's claim and your doctor's claim are not necessarily opposites — one may be referring to complete restoration, the other to partial or short-term improvement. The disagreement may partly be about what 'helps' means.
treat_skeptically: Any sleep recommendation framed as an exact universal number — the precision is the part that goes beyond what a population average can establish.
Single-person testimonials for sleep products or interventions, including blue light glasses — a reported improvement in one case does not isolate the cause or generalize to others.
Absolute claims in either direction about weekend sleep recovery — 'cannot be repaid at all' and 'fully restores everything lost' are both stronger than the question currently supports.
what_would_change_the_answer: Whether individuals' sleep requirements cluster reliably around a narrow range or span a wider one would sharpen the '8 hours exactly' question — and that distinction is not settled by the '8 hours' rule itself.

Evidence comparing pre-bed blue light filtering against a control condition, using defined sleep outcomes, would help distinguish whether the filtering itself drives any benefit or whether other factors account for reported improvements.

Evidence distinguishing partial short-term recovery from full restoration of prior sleep loss — and whether circadian timing effects from shifted weekend sleep offset any recovery benefit — would help resolve what your friend and doctor are actually disagreeing about.

sources_of_noise.source_type: Population average converted to individual rule
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A figure that describes a group — an average, a guideline, a rough range — gets restated as a precise requirement applying equally to every individual. The variation within the group disappears, and the average becomes a universal standard.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: An exact number is stated as universally required, without acknowledging that it comes from a distribution where individuals differ. Words like 'exactly,' 'everyone,' and 'or your health suffers' are signs the original estimate has been tightened beyond what it supports.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A question that has not been resolved — whether sleep loss can be recovered, and how completely — gets presented as having a clear answer, usually whichever position the speaker holds. Both sides can do this simultaneously, each presenting one position as the obvious truth.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Two sources give flatly contradictory answers with equal confidence, and neither acknowledges the other's position or explains what evidence would settle the disagreement.

output.topic_as_understood: Whether everyone requires exactly 8 hours of sleep, whether blue-light glasses resolve insomnia, and whether lost sleep can be recovered on weekends
output.framing: Each of these claims conflates a population-level pattern or average with a precise universal rule. The useful question is not whether a single number applies to everyone, but what the claims themselves actually establish versus what they assume.

items.claim: A single fixed sleep requirement does not follow from the observation that most adults function well within a broad range of nightly sleep
items.basis: By definition, a population average or typical range cannot establish a precise universal requirement. The claim 'everyone needs exactly 8 hours' asserts both a precise number and a universal application — either would need independent support, and together they compound the problem. The logic of individual biological variation makes a single fixed number implausible as a hard rule for all adults.
items.limits: This does not establish what the actual range is, how much it varies, or what the consequences of falling below any particular threshold are for any specific person.

items.claim: The 'sleep debt' metaphor does not by itself establish that lost sleep accumulates hour-for-hour, that recovery works hour-for-hour, or that a specific amount of weekend sleep fully restores a prior state
items.basis: This follows from analyzing what the metaphor does and does not establish. A debt metaphor is compatible with many different repayment structures — partial, full, asymmetric, time-limited — so the metaphor alone cannot settle the dispute between your friend and your doctor. Their disagreement is a genuine empirical question, not one resolvable by the logic of the framing itself.
items.limits: This does not tell you which view is correct — it identifies that the metaphor cannot decide it.

still_worth_verifying.question: To what extent, and under what conditions, does sleep lost across a week return to baseline after additional sleep on subsequent days — and does the answer differ for different outcomes (mood, reaction time, metabolic markers)?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: This is exactly the empirical dispute between your friend and your doctor, and the metaphor analysis cannot resolve it — only evidence tracking specific outcomes before and after recovery sleep could.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Controlled comparisons measuring specific functional outcomes after sleep restriction followed by extended recovery sleep, across different deficit sizes and recovery durations.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does filtering blue-spectrum light before sleep reliably improve sleep onset or sleep quality as a general intervention, independent of other behavioral changes made at the same time?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Your coworker's experience with blue-light glasses is a single case where multiple things may have changed simultaneously — including attention to sleep habits — so the glasses specifically cannot be credited without isolating their effect.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Comparisons of sleep outcomes with and without blue-light filtering that hold other pre-sleep behaviors constant, using defined sleep measures rather than self-report alone.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether you personally function well, poorly, or adequately on less or more than 8 hours — that depends on your own observed functioning, not a population figure.
Whether blue-light glasses would help your sleep specifically, given that your coworker's improvement could reflect habit changes, expectation effects, or the glasses themselves.
Whether catching up on weekends is a workable strategy for you depends on the size of any deficit you are carrying, what outcomes matter to you, and information this analysis does not have.
